research.answer:
The question was matched to: microgravity, material flammability. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.

**Evidence**
- BASS: 1-g material screening is not automatically conservative. Spacecraft material selection relies on NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which ranks materials by 1-g behaviour. BASS and BASS-II were built on the hypothesis that, with adequate ventilation, materials burn as well if not better… [S1]
- BASS-II: 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. [S2]
- BASS: Flame spread and extinction over realistic solid fuels (cotton-fiberglass fabric, PMMA in several geometries, Nomex) in low-speed forced flow aboard the ISS. Built to bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 screening method and real microgravity flammability, and… [S3]
- BASS-II: flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given… [S4]
- STDCE-1: Microgravity Experiments [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S10]
- BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations  [S11]

**Limits**
- Extractive answer (no language model configured): passages are quoted, not interpreted.
- Only documents in this knowledge base were searched.

sources.title: Cool flames: combustion at 500–1000 K
sources.text: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of about 500–1000 K. FLEX, CFI and CFI-G studied them on droplets and burners in microgravity. Limitation: Research fuels and configurations; relevance to cabin fires is an open question, not a finding.

Flames did spread in microgravity over: PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric). Limitation: One test per configuration; single flow speed and near-normal O2.

results.title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
why: Data: 2 test-level records.

top_passage.text: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions.
